Fireflies.ai Meeting Transcript

Title: Northbridge AI x Redwood — Hosted Rollouts (percentage canary) workflow demo
Date/Time: 2024-10-02 10:00 PT
Duration: 46 min
Meeting ID: ff_9f31c2

Attendees
- Miguel Santos (Redwood) — Account / customer success
- Dylan Brooks (Redwood) — Console engineering lead
- Logan Wright (Redwood) — Telemetry lead
- Ava Chen (Northbridge) — VP Engineering
- Rohan Gupta (Northbridge) — ML Platform
- Megan O'Neil (Northbridge) — Security
- Samir Khan (Northbridge) — SRE

Auto-summary (generated)
- Northbridge wants a safe percentage-based canary workflow on Hosted routes to roll model version changes without causing production incidents.
- Redwood demoed the Console rollout wizard: baseline vs candidate selection, percentage steps (manual + timed), guardrails (latency, error rate, token cost deltas), preview effective routing, activity timeline, and one-click pause/rollback.
- Key questions: guardrail enforcement behavior, sticky routing/session semantics for streaming, per-variant monitoring + metric cardinality, and audit log completeness (diffs, actor attribution, exports).

Topics
- Creating a rollout on a Hosted route (baseline vs candidate)
- Percentage traffic splitting + step schedules
- Sticky routing options and streaming/session semantics
- Guardrails: latency/error/cost + optional quality gates
- Monitoring: baseline vs candidate compare dashboards
- Audit logging and RBAC/entitlements

Questions captured
- If we set 5% candidate, how do you ensure a user/session doesn’t “flip-flop” between variants mid conversation?
- What happens to in-flight streaming responses if we hit pause/rollback?
- Are guardrails “hard stops” (auto-pause) or just alerting? Can we require guardrails before 100%?
- Can we see per-variant p95 latency and 5xx rate, and can we alert on the delta vs baseline?
- Do audit logs include before/after diffs of weights and model versions, and can we export to Splunk?

Action items
- Miguel: send docs + screenshots and confirm GA timeline for Northbridge
- Dylan: send Loom video of rollback/pause + audit history view
- Logan: share metric list + dashboard panels + cardinality guidance
- Northbridge: share their traffic pattern and monitoring thresholds

Transcript

[00:00] Miguel Santos: Alright, we’re at the top of the hour. Thanks everyone for joining. Today Dylan is gonna walk through the Hosted rollouts, the percentage canary workflow in the Console, and then Logan can cover what the monitoring looks like. Does that sound good?

[00:14] Ava Chen: Yep, perfect.

[00:16] Rohan Gupta: Yeah. We mainly want to understand, like, can we do a real canary and not just, you know, a flag that randomly breaks prod.

[00:23] Miguel Santos: Totally hear you. Maybe quick context from your side first? What are you doing today for rollouts?

[00:30] Samir Khan: We basically do “new model version” in staging, then when we flip in prod it’s… honestly it’s kind of all-at-once. We can do some routing at our edge but it’s messy, and it doesn’t understand streaming sessions.

[00:45] Megan O'Neil: And we don’t have an audit trail for the change beyond, like, a Git commit and whoever ran the pipeline.

[00:52] Miguel Santos: Got it. That maps exactly to what this feature is aimed at. Dylan, want to take over and share screen?

[00:59] Dylan Brooks: Yep, sharing now.

[01:04] Dylan Brooks: Okay, can you all see the Redwood Console? I’m in a demo org. On the left nav there’s “Hosted Routes.” I’ll click into a route called “chat-prod-us.”

[01:17] Ava Chen: Yep, we see it.

[01:19] Dylan Brooks: Cool. So under the route, there’s a “Rollouts” tab. If there’s no active rollout, you’ll see an empty state with “Create rollout.” I’ll click that.

[01:31] Dylan Brooks: The wizard starts with selecting baseline and candidate. Baseline is what you’re running today — here it’s “Llama-3.1-70B-instruct v3.2” — and candidate might be “v3.3” or a different quant profile or sometimes a different model family.

[01:48] Rohan Gupta: So is that model “version” the thing you pin? Like, if upstream changes kernels you don’t change us?

[01:55] Dylan Brooks: Yeah, exactly. For Hosted, a “version” here is a pinned Redwood serving build + model artifact, not like “latest.” So you can control the change.

[02:05] Miguel Santos: That’s also relevant for compliance folks — it’s immutable from your perspective.

[02:10] Megan O'Neil: Good.

[02:12] Dylan Brooks: Next step is traffic split. By default we start conservative: 1% candidate, 99% baseline. You can do manual steps, like 1 → 5 → 10 → 25 → 50 → 100. Or timed progression. I’ll click “timed” to show it — you can say “move to next step every 30 minutes” if guardrails are healthy.

[02:35] Samir Khan: So it can auto-advance? That’s the part that scares me a bit.

[02:39] Dylan Brooks: Yeah, and it’s optional. Also you can require “pass” conditions. The guardrails come next.

[02:47] Dylan Brooks: Guardrails: you can set thresholds for error rate (like 5xx + upstream timeouts), latency, and token cost deltas. Here we’re showing p95 latency threshold: “candidate p95 must be <= baseline p95 + 20%” — that’s a common pattern. Error rate might be “candidate 5xx <= 1% and not more than +0.5% vs baseline.”

[03:12] Ava Chen: Are these defaults or do we choose?

[03:15] Dylan Brooks: You choose, but we’ll provide recommended presets. We’ve been leaning toward safe defaults, especially for the “don’t let someone set 100% with nothing.”

[03:23] Megan O'Neil: Is it enforced? Like it blocks you?

[03:26] Dylan Brooks: There are two parts: validation at create/update time, and runtime behavior. For GA, the plan is: if you try to schedule to 100% candidate, we can require guardrails or admin permission depending on your plan/entitlements. And at runtime, if guardrails trip, we can auto-pause and alert.

[03:47] Logan Wright: Slight nuance — some folks start with “alert only” during beta, but GA is moving toward “policy can pause.” The exact behavior is configurable.

[03:55] Rohan Gupta: When you say auto-pause, is that like “set candidate to zero” or “freeze at current weight”?

[04:02] Dylan Brooks: Good question. Pause means “stop changing the schedule” and optionally “freeze weights.” Most customers want “freeze” first, then decide. Rollback is the explicit action to force baseline 100%.

[04:17] Samir Khan: I’d want a big red button that sets candidate to zero, honestly.

[04:21] Dylan Brooks: That’s rollback. Also there’s “Emergency rollback” which is basically the same but with fewer confirmation steps, depending on RBAC.

[04:31] Miguel Santos: Speaking of, we can cover RBAC after the demo.

[04:35] Dylan Brooks: Next part: “Preview effective routing.” This is important if you have layered policies, like account-level constraints or region overrides. The preview endpoint resolves what will actually happen per region.

[04:49] Ava Chen: We had an issue with another vendor where the UI said 10% but one region was like 30.

[04:54] Dylan Brooks: Yeah, exactly. Here you can click “Preview” and see: us-east-1 95/5, eu-west-1 95/5, etc. If a region is out of date, it’ll show staleness and the last applied version.

[05:10] Samir Khan: That’s great. How real-time is that?

[05:13] Dylan Brooks: Typically seconds, but it depends on propagation. We have SLOs around staleness. Logan/Allison from SRE define those, but you’ll get an indicator.

[05:24] Logan Wright: We also emit a change event when the policy is applied in each region, which helps debugging.

[05:31] Dylan Brooks: Now, “Activity.” When you create/update/pause/rollback, it’s recorded in an audit timeline. I’ll jump there.

[05:40] Dylan Brooks: This shows “Rollout created by Dylan (demo)” at timestamp, with a diff: baseline model/version, candidate model/version, the step schedule, and guardrails.

[05:52] Megan O'Neil: Does it include who did it even if it’s via API?

[05:56] Dylan Brooks: Yes, actor attribution includes API keys, service accounts, SSO users. And IP address when applicable.

[06:05] Megan O'Neil: And can we export this to Splunk?

[06:09] Miguel Santos: We have a few options — we can ship to your SIEM via webhook or export to S3 and then Splunk can ingest. Kevin on our security team can confirm exact formats. But yes, audit logs are first-class here.

[06:23] Megan O'Neil: Okay. We’ll need that in writing.

[06:26] Miguel Santos: Yep, action item for us.

[06:29] Dylan Brooks: Let me back up to the routing semantics because it’s usually the tricky part. There’s a toggle for “sticky routing.” Default is non-sticky weighted random per request. Sticky means we hash a stable key, usually like user_id or session_id if you provide it, and that deterministically maps to baseline or candidate.

[06:52] Rohan Gupta: For us, it’s chat sessions. We do streaming and tool calls. If request one goes to baseline and request two goes to candidate, you basically ruin evals.

[07:01] Dylan Brooks: Exactly. For streaming, we pin the variant at request start, and retries reuse it. For multi-turn, you can pass a session key to keep consistency.

[07:13] Samir Khan: Is that the same as “request hash”? Or do we have to plumb something?

[07:18] Dylan Brooks: You can do either. If you do nothing, it’s best-effort per request. If you send `x-redwood-sticky-key` (name might be slightly different, sorry), then it will stick across calls.

[07:31] Logan Wright: And from telemetry perspective, stickiness helps reduce noise in comparing baseline vs candidate.

[07:38] Ava Chen: Does stickiness hurt caching? Like prefix caching?

[07:42] Dylan Brooks: It can. If you stick too hard, you might reduce cross-tenant cache hits. That’s why it’s optional and you choose the key granularity.

[07:54] Rohan Gupta: Okay.

[07:56] Dylan Brooks: Let’s talk about streaming rollback because you asked earlier: if you rollback during an in-flight stream, we do not cut the stream mid-response. That stream continues on its pinned variant. New requests will route to baseline after the rollback is applied.

[08:14] Samir Khan: So there’s a delay until it takes effect.

[08:17] Dylan Brooks: It’s basically “effective immediately for new requests,” but in-flight is in-flight.

[08:23] Samir Khan: That’s fine.

[08:25] Megan O'Neil: Is that documented? Because people panic if they click rollback and still see candidate traffic for a minute.

[08:31] Miguel Santos: Yeah, we should include that in the runbook and docs. We’ll share.

[08:36] Logan Wright: You’ll also see it in metrics: streams started before rollback will still be tagged candidate.

[08:43] Dylan Brooks: Speaking of metrics, Logan, want to show the dashboard?

[08:47] Logan Wright: Sure. I’ll share my screen.

[08:52] Logan Wright: Okay, this is the canary compare dashboard. The main thing is we break down by variant: baseline vs candidate. Dimensions include route, region, and variant. We’re careful about cardinality — we don’t explode on arbitrary customer IDs.

[09:11] Samir Khan: Thank you. Our last vendor basically blew up Prometheus.

[09:15] Logan Wright: Yeah, same scars. So the dashboard shows request count, error rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, and token cost. Cost is “input tokens,” “output tokens,” and estimated $ per 1k tokens. For canary, we show deltas like “candidate minus baseline.”

[09:36] Ava Chen: Can we alert on that delta?

[09:38] Logan Wright: Yes. We have recommended alerts: candidate 5xx rate > baseline by X for Y minutes; candidate p95 latency > baseline by X%; and token cost delta > threshold.

[09:52] Rohan Gupta: What about quality? Like, we have offline evals.

[09:56] Logan Wright: There’s an optional “quality gate” integration. It’s not always fully automated for Hosted. The GA version supports wiring in eval signals — like your own score — and then you can treat it as a guardrail input. But a lot of folks start with latency + errors + cost.

[10:15] Rohan Gupta: Okay, we’re probably in that camp.

[10:18] Megan O'Neil: I care about audit logs and access. Like who can do rollback. We don’t want every engineer to push 100% candidate.

[10:26] Miguel Santos: Yep. RBAC: there are permissions like “create rollout,” “edit rollout,” “pause,” “rollback.” Typically “rollback” is broader because it’s a safety action, but “edit” might be restricted.

[10:40] Dylan Brooks: Also you can gate the entire feature by plan, but within your org, roles determine who sees the wizard and who can click what.

[10:50] Megan O'Neil: SSO required?

[10:52] Miguel Santos: For enterprise plans, yes, we support SAML/SSO. For this workflow, you can also require SSO session for sensitive actions. We can follow up with our security team.

[11:06] Ava Chen: Going back to guardrails — if someone sets 50% candidate and it starts erroring, do you auto rollback or auto pause?

[11:14] Dylan Brooks: Default is auto pause, then you decide to rollback. Some customers do auto rollback if error rate is severe. We’re being careful because auto rollback could thrash if metrics are noisy.

[11:29] Samir Khan: What’s the evaluation window? Like 1 minute? 5 minutes?

[11:32] Logan Wright: Configurable. We recommend at least 5 minutes for latency and error unless you have huge QPS. There’s also min sample size so you don’t pause on like 10 requests.

[11:47] Rohan Gupta: Is the policy evaluation deterministic? Like, we’ve seen weirdness where two gateways disagree.

[11:54] Dylan Brooks: That’s an explicit requirement. Policy evaluation is deterministic and versioned. The preview shows the resolved version; the data plane uses the same evaluation. Also we do monotonic versions so regions don’t apply older weights after newer ones.

[12:12] Samir Khan: Nice.

[12:13] Ava Chen: Can you show edit flow? Like, if we want to change from 10% to 5%.

[12:18] Dylan Brooks: Yep. Back to the rollout page — there’s “Edit rollout.” When you change weights or schedule, you get a confirmation screen that shows the diff. And it writes an audit entry.

[12:32] Megan O'Neil: The diff is important. Like “before/after.”

[12:35] Dylan Brooks: Exactly.

[12:37] Logan Wright: And for telemetry, the “change events” annotate the charts. So you’ll see vertical lines like “Step changed to 10% at 10:12.”

[12:48] Samir Khan: Love that.

[12:50] Rohan Gupta: Another question: We do multiple regions. Can we canary in one region first?

[12:56] Dylan Brooks: Yes, you can scope rollout to regions if your plan supports it. Or you can create a route per region and roll them separately. But the workflow supports region filters.

[13:11] Ava Chen: Okay.

[13:12] Megan O'Neil: What about data retention? Are prompts stored?

[13:16] Miguel Santos: By default we don’t store prompt/response bodies for Hosted unless you enable logging features. For audit logs, we store change metadata, not the content. The audit event will say “model version changed” and “weights changed,” but not the user prompt.

[13:33] Megan O'Neil: Good. But do you include route names? That might contain internal IDs.

[13:38] Dylan Brooks: Route names are included, yeah. If that’s a concern we can recommend naming patterns. Also the audit payload is configurable in terms of redaction for some fields.

[13:50] Megan O'Neil: Okay.

[13:52] Logan Wright: On the metrics side, we also avoid high-cardinality fields. Route is the main one. Variant is just baseline/candidate. Model version is a bounded label.

[14:06] Rohan Gupta: Can we canary multiple candidates? Like A/B/C?

[14:10] Dylan Brooks: For this workflow, it’s baseline + one candidate. Multi-variant experimentation is on the roadmap, but GA is focused on safe rollouts.

[14:20] Ava Chen: That’s fine. We just need canary.

[14:23] Miguel Santos: And honestly most teams start with one candidate for risk control.

[14:28] Samir Khan: What about rate limits and quotas? If candidate is slower, does it starve baseline?

[14:35] Dylan Brooks: The weighting happens at routing, then each variant has capacity management behind it. For Hosted, we manage the pools, but you’ll see if candidate is saturating and causing queueing. Guardrails should catch that.

[14:51] Logan Wright: We also have a “throttled requests” panel and queue time. If candidate starts queueing, you’ll see latency change decomposition.

[15:03] Ava Chen: Great.

[15:05] Miguel Santos: Let’s pause and see if there are other questions before we jump to next steps.

[15:10] Rohan Gupta: One more: When you say “token cost delta,” how accurate is that? Because providers sometimes do weird stuff.

[15:18] Logan Wright: It’s based on measured tokens in/out and your configured price for that model version. So it’s consistent within Redwood. If you compare across vendors it’s apples/oranges. But for baseline vs candidate inside Redwood, it’s reliable.

[15:34] Samir Khan: And does it include retries?

[15:36] Logan Wright: Yes, if a request retries, it’s counted. That’s actually why error guardrails are important — retries inflate cost.

[15:47] Megan O'Neil: Audit logs again — do you log read access? Like someone viewing the rollout?

[15:53] Miguel Santos: For GA we’re focused on change events. Read events can be available in some compliance tiers, but we need to confirm. Most compliance asks are “who changed routing.”

[16:05] Megan O'Neil: Okay, but please confirm.

[16:08] Miguel Santos: Will do.

[16:10] Dylan Brooks: Also quick note: there’s an “Export history” button in the UI, which gives you a CSV of the timeline. Not a replacement for SIEM export, but useful.

[16:22] Ava Chen: Nice.

[16:24] Miguel Santos: Cool. I’ll summarize what I heard as success criteria for you: (1) safe percentage rollouts on Hosted, (2) guardrails that can pause/rollback, (3) stable routing for streaming sessions, (4) monitoring with baseline vs candidate compare, and (5) audit logs with before/after diffs and export. That accurate?

[16:45] Ava Chen: Yes.

[16:46] Rohan Gupta: Yep.

[16:47] Megan O'Neil: Yep.

[16:50] Samir Khan: Yes.

[16:52] Miguel Santos: Great. Next steps from our side: I’ll send a docs draft plus screenshots. Dylan will send a Loom showing pause/rollback and the preview routing. Logan will share the metrics and dashboard spec with recommended alerts.

[17:09] Miguel Santos: From your side, can you send us your typical traffic pattern — like QPS, percent streaming, and what you use as a “session key,” if any. That’ll help us recommend stickiness settings.

[17:21] Rohan Gupta: Yeah, I can send that.

[17:23] Samir Khan: I’ll add some SRE notes, like our latency SLO.

[17:27] Miguel Santos: Perfect. And Megan, you mentioned Splunk — if you can confirm whether you want Splunk HEC, S3 export, or webhook, we can loop in our security engineer with the right answer.

[17:40] Megan O'Neil: I’ll check internally.

[17:42] Miguel Santos: Awesome.

[17:44] Ava Chen: Can we also get a sense of timeline? Like when this is GA.

[17:49] Miguel Santos: We’re targeting GA soon; it’s currently in the final hardening stage. I’ll follow up with the current ETA and whether we can get you into a limited beta earlier.

[18:02] Ava Chen: Great.

[18:04] Miguel Santos: Alright, thanks all. We’ll follow up by tomorrow with the materials. Anything else before we drop?

[18:12] (crosstalk)

[18:14] Samir Khan: Nope, good.

[18:16] Rohan Gupta: All set.

[18:17] Megan O'Neil: Thanks.

[18:19] Miguel Santos: Thank you.

[Note: Fireflies transcription ended early; meeting continued briefly for scheduling and calendar holds.]
